explanations.explanation: True, friend. The LORD says He is doing this “that you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians when I performed miraculous signs among them” (Exodus 10:2). So these signs are meant to be handed down at the family table, like a recipe that never gets lost. And the point of the telling is “so that all of you may know that I am the LORD.” (Exodus 10:2)

Look at verse 2 again, friend. The LORD says He is doing this “that you may tell your children and grandchildren” what happened (Exodus 10:2). So the signs aren't only about that one day with Pharaoh. They're a story meant to be told to the next generations, and a story like that gets told a LOT.

Locusts, friend. The LORD says, “I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow.” (Exodus 10:4). Tomorrow! That's a one-day warning, which is more notice than my cookie timer gives me, and it always dings right when my hands are full of dough.

Frogs already had their turn earlier, when they came up and covered the land (Exodus 8:6). This time the LORD says, “I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow.” (Exodus 10:4). Same land, brand new visitors, and these ones come with a date on the calendar.

Gnats were an earlier plague, when all the dust of the land became gnats (Exodus 8:17). For this one, the LORD says, “I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow.” (Exodus 10:4). Tiny bugs, big bugs, Egypt keeps getting a new kind every time.

explanations.answer: Whatever is left after the hail
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, “They will devour whatever is left after the hail” and “eat every tree that grows in your fields” (Exodus 10:5). The hail took the first swing, and the locusts come for whatever is still standing. When verse 12 repeats it, it calls this “everything that the hail has left behind.” (Exodus 10:12)

Storehouses aren't mentioned here. The LORD says, “They will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields.” (Exodus 10:5). So the target is what's out on the land after the hail already came through, plus the trees.

Reeds along the Nile don't show up in this warning. The LORD says, “They will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields.” (Exodus 10:5). The hail goes first in that sentence, and the locusts come for whatever it left.

Pharaoh's officials, friend. The text says, “Pharaoh’s officials asked him, ‘How long will this man be a snare to us?’” (Exodus 10:7). It's like the whole office walking up to the boss's desk together. I think that's not a walk anybody takes lightly.

The magicians don't show up in this passage at all. Verse 7 says, “Pharaoh’s officials asked him, ‘How long will this man be a snare to us?’” (Exodus 10:7). The voices pushing back on Pharaoh come from his own officials.

Pharaoh's daughter isn't in this passage. The text says, “Pharaoh’s officials asked him, ‘How long will this man be a snare to us?’” (Exodus 10:7). So no family meeting here, just the people who work for him speaking up.

True. His officials say, “Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God.” (Exodus 10:7). Notice they say “the LORD their God.” Unsolicited advice from the staff, but this time it's worth listening to.

Check verse 7 again, friend. His officials say, “Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God.” (Exodus 10:7). So they aren't telling him to hold on to the people, they're telling him to let them go.

Right on, baker. Pharaoh says, “Go, worship the LORD your God,” and then asks, “But who exactly will be going?” (Exodus 10:8). That's the guy who says “sure, borrow my ladder” and then wants to know who else is coming. The yes and the question show up in the same breath.

explanations.answer: How many days they will be gone
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh doesn't ask about days. After “Go, worship the LORD your God,” he asks, “But who exactly will be going?” (Exodus 10:8). His question is about the people, not about the calendar.
Pharaoh doesn't ask about the place. After “Go, worship the LORD your God,” he asks, “But who exactly will be going?” (Exodus 10:8). It's the guest list he wants, not the address.

That's it, friend. Moses answers, “We will go with our young and old,” and adds, “with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds” (Exodus 10:9). No cutoff, no short list. When Moses answers, he leaves nobody out.

Moses doesn't narrow it to tribe leaders. He says, “We will go with our young and old,” and also “with our sons and daughters” (Exodus 10:9). It's the whole people he's talking about, not just the top of the list.

Moses doesn't name the Levites here. He says, “We will go with our young and old,” and adds, “with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds” (Exodus 10:9). The answer covers everyone, not one family group.

Men, friend. Pharaoh says, “No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting.” (Exodus 10:11). Moses had said sons, daughters, young and old (Exodus 10:9), so Pharaoh cuts that list way down. It's like asking for a full batch and getting handed one cookie.

Elders aren't the word Pharaoh uses. He says, “No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting.” (Exodus 10:11). Moses had asked for far more than that (Exodus 10:9). Pharaoh's answer is about the men.

Priests aren't mentioned in Pharaoh's answer. He says, “No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting.” (Exodus 10:11). Moses had asked for the sons and daughters to come too (Exodus 10:9). Pharaoh's counteroffer is just the men.

East, baker. The text says, “throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts.” (Exodus 10:13). A whole day and night of wind, and then the locusts arrive. I'd call that a forecast nobody wanted.

Not south. Verse 13 says, “throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land.” (Exodus 10:13). That east wind is what “had brought the locusts” by morning. Keep your compass pointed east for this one.

Not north. The text says the LORD sent “an east wind across the land,” and it went on throughout that day and night (Exodus 10:13). By morning, “the east wind had brought the locusts.” (Exodus 10:13). North doesn't get a mention.

Not a few, friend. The text says, “Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 10:15). That means no holdouts, and no one lonely little leaf. I've seen picked-over cookie plates with more left on them.

False is right, baker. The text says, “Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 10:15). Not a few plants, not one stubborn tree. I've seen picked-over cookie plates with more left on them.

Sinned, friend. Pharaoh says, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.” (Exodus 10:16). It's a short sentence, and it names God and Moses both. Those are big words coming from the king.

Boasted is a fair guess for a king, but it's not what he says. Verse 16 has him say, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.” (Exodus 10:16). In that sentence he isn't bragging, he's saying something much humbler.
Grumbled isn't the word. Pharaoh says, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.” (Exodus 10:16). No complaining in that sentence, just that one plain word: sinned.

explanations.answer: Forgive him and appeal to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Pharaoh says, “Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me.” (Exodus 10:17). Look at that, the word “please” just showed up. It's been missing for a while.

explanations.answer: Leave Egypt before the next sunrise
explanations.explanation: That's not what he asks. Pharaoh says, “Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me.” (Exodus 10:17). He's asking for forgiveness and for Moses to appeal to the LORD, not for anyone to go.

explanations.answer: Bring him an offering for the LORD
explanations.explanation: No offering is mentioned in his request. Pharaoh says, “Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me.” (Exodus 10:17). His ask is forgiveness and an appeal to the LORD.

explanations.answer: Changes it to a very strong west wind
explanations.explanation: West wind, friend. The text says the LORD “changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea.” (Exodus 10:19). East wind in, west wind out, like a revolving door. And it all happens after Moses appeals to the LORD (Exodus 10:18).

explanations.answer: Stops it completely for a whole day
explanations.explanation: The wind doesn't stop. Verse 19 says the LORD “changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea.” (Exodus 10:19). A very strong wind, the other direction. That's a lot of wind for a day that supposedly goes still.

explanations.answer: Turns it into a heavy rainstorm
explanations.explanation: No rainstorm in this verse. The text says the LORD “changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea.” (Exodus 10:19). The wind itself did the job.
True, friend. The text says, “Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt.” (Exodus 10:19). Not one straggler stuck in a corner of a house. Considering how thick they were, that's quite a cleanup.
Check verse 19 again, friend. It says, “Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt.” (Exodus 10:19). Not one straggler, anywhere. The wind carried them off into the Red Sea.

Three, baker. The text says, “total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days.” (Exodus 10:22). Three days with no light to find the light switch. I'd be walking into my own ovens by hour two.
Not seven. The text says, “total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days.” (Exodus 10:22). Three days is plenty already. I'd bump into my own ovens before the first day was over.
Forty is a big number, but not the one here. The text says, “total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days.” (Exodus 10:22). Three days of darkness, and that's already a lot.

Not quite, friend. Verse 23 says, “Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings.” (Exodus 10:23). So Egypt couldn't see a thing, and the Israelites' homes still had light. It's like a power outage that somehow skips certain houses.

False is right. The text says, “Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings.” (Exodus 10:23). While all the land of Egypt was in total darkness, the Israelites still had light in their homes. Same land, very different lighting.

That's it, baker. Pharaoh says, “Go, worship the LORD. Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind.” (Exodus 10:24). He gives a little and keeps the livestock. It's like saying you can borrow the car but the keys stay here.
Carts and tools aren't in his offer. Pharaoh says, “Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind.” (Exodus 10:24). The animals are what he wants to keep.
Gold and silver aren't mentioned in this offer. Pharaoh says, “Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind.” (Exodus 10:24). The animals are what he holds back.

explanations.answer: They'll need some of them to worship the LORD
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Moses says, “not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God” (Exodus 10:26). Not a hoof! Moses counts hooves the way I count chocolate chips, and nothing gets skipped.

explanations.answer: The herds would wander off without them
explanations.explanation: Wandering isn't Moses' reason. He says, “not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God” (Exodus 10:26). The reason has to do with worship.

explanations.answer: The animals are too weak to stay behind
explanations.explanation: Weak animals aren't part of what Moses says. He says, “not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God” (Exodus 10:26). Worship is the reason he gives.

Look at the end of verse 26. Moses says, “we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive.” (Exodus 10:26). So they don't have the whole plan in hand before they leave. It's like packing for a trip and finding out the details when you land.

False, friend. Moses says, “we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive.” (Exodus 10:26). So they don't know how before they leave. It's like packing for a trip and finding out the details when you land.
Die, friend. Pharaoh says, “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.” (Exodus 10:28). I think this one is heavy. It's a king threatening a man's life.
Kneeling isn't what Pharaoh says. He says, “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.” (Exodus 10:28). It's a threat on Moses' life.
Paying isn't what Pharaoh says. He says, “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.” (Exodus 10:28). That's a threat, plain and serious.

explanations.answer: He agrees with what Pharaoh said
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses replies, “As you say,” and then, “I will never see your face again.” (Exodus 10:29). I think there's a steadiness in those few words. He doesn't argue the threat and he doesn't plead.

explanations.answer: He begs Pharaoh for one more meeting
explanations.explanation: No begging in verse 29. Moses replies, “As you say,” and then, “I will never see your face again.” (Exodus 10:29). He agrees with what Pharaoh said instead of asking for more time.

explanations.answer: He sends Aaron back in his place
explanations.explanation: Aaron isn't sent in verse 29. Moses answers for himself: “As you say,” and then, “I will never see your face again.” (Exodus 10:29). He agrees with Pharaoh's words.
